title: Fenwick trees, segment trees, and static range queries
concepts: A range-query structure preprocesses or organizes values so queries over subarrays can be answered faster than scanning every element, often while supporting updates.
A Fenwick tree stores partial prefix aggregates indexed by the lowest set bit; point updates and prefix sums take O(log n), and range sums follow by subtracting two prefixes.
A segment tree recursively stores an aggregate for each interval; point updates and associative range queries take O(log n), and the combine operation defines the supported aggregate.
Lazy propagation stores deferred range updates at internal nodes and pushes them only when a child must be visited; update composition and query semantics must be defined precisely.

A sparse table precomputes power-of-two intervals; idempotent operations such as min or max can answer static range queries in O(1), while general associative operations need a different query decomposition.

Prefix sums suit static additive data, Fenwick trees suit compact additive updates and prefix queries, segment trees support broader associative aggregates and updates, and sparse tables favor static idempotent queries.
Coordinate compression preserves ordering among a known finite set of coordinates and can make Fenwick or segment trees feasible when original values are huge.
Indexing convention, inclusive versus half-open ranges, identity values, and non-power-of-two sizes are common implementation errors; test single-element and full-range queries.
